title: Delhi Pollution Data Went Missing at Several Stations as Diwali Peak Hit
excerpt: Readings blanked for hours on Deepavali night while PM2.5 climbed past 900 at stations that kept reporting. A Congress leader says 25 of 39 stations recorded nothing between 2 a.m. and 3 a.m.
body:
• Air quality readings went blank at several government monitoring stations in Delhi for hours on Deepavali night, just as firecracker pollution peaked, according to The Hindu and other reports.
  • RK Puram's PM2.5 reading reached 924 micrograms per cubic metre at 9 p.m. before the station stopped displaying data; the JNU station, which kept reporting, hit 786 by 11 p.m.
  • Congress leader Ajay Maken said 25 of Delhi's 39 comparable stations recorded no PM2.5 data between 2 a.m. and 3 a.m., while the nine stations that did report averaged 576 micrograms per cubic metre — 38.4 times the WHO 24-hour limit he cited.
  • Delhi's overall AQI was 370, in the "very poor" category, on Monday morning. Missing hourly PM2.5 data can artificially lower the AQI, The Hindu reported.

At the peak of Deepavali night pollution in Delhi, the data itself went missing. Air quality readings went blank for several monitoring stations for many hours, The Hindu reported, as firecrackers pushed pollution to its worst levels of the festival — raising questions about what the city's true peak actually was.

The gaps appeared on the websites of the Delhi Pollution Control Committee (DPCC) and the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), the two authorities whose networks feed the official Air Quality Index. The Hindu noted the mechanical consequence: when hourly PM2.5 data is missing, it can artificially lower the AQI that residents and officials rely on.

What the surviving data showed

The stations that kept reporting recorded extreme levels. RK Puram's PM2.5 concentration climbed to 924 micrograms per cubic metre by 9 p.m. before its readings stopped, according to reports tracking the DPCC feed. The Jawaharlal Nehru University station continued publishing and showed PM2.5 rising from 161 micrograms per cubic metre at 8 p.m. to 786 by 11 p.m. — nearly five times higher in three hours. The stations named as going dark in multiple reports include RK Puram, Nehru Nagar, Mundka, Sonia Vihar and Dwarka.

The Hindu BusinessLine, citing wire reporting, said at least 44 of the CPCB's 59 stations failed to show particulate-matter readings, that PM2.5 topped 900 micrograms per cubic metre at several locations — more than 60 times the WHO level it referenced — and that more than 50 stations recorded peaks above 300. Manoj Kumar, an analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, told the paper some anomaly occurred as PM2.5 levels approached the monitors' upper limit of 1,000 micrograms per cubic metre, raising the possibility that official averages understated the episode.

The political charge, and the unanswered question

Senior Congress leader Ajay Maken, citing CPCB data in a post on X, said no PM2.5 readings were recorded at 25 of the 39 stations with comparable data between 2 a.m. and 3 a.m. on the night of November 8–9, and that the nine stations with data in both years averaged 576 micrograms per cubic metre in that hour. He listed the affected stations, which included Anand Vihar, Ashok Vihar, Bawana, Dwarka Sector 8, ITO, Mundka, Punjabi Bagh, RK Puram and Wazirpur.

None of the reports read for this article carried an official explanation from the DPCC or CPCB for the outages, and the reason for the interruptions has not been independently established. Similar interruptions during peak pollution hours have been reported in earlier Diwali seasons, according to the same coverage.

What it means for residents

On Monday morning, Delhi's overall AQI stood at 370 — "very poor" — with 20 stations in the "severe" band and Sonia Vihar highest at 463, according to CPCB figures reported by Dainik Jagran. Independent platforms reported far higher real-time peaks overnight, which is precisely the problem the missing data creates: the official record of the year's worst pollution night has holes in it, and the averages built from it may flatter the night.
